value.overview: The Masked Tityra (Tityra semifasciata) is a medium-sized passerine of tropical forests and woodland edges in the Americas. It is a conspicuous bird with pale gray plumage, a dark facial mask, red skin around the eye, and a pinkish-red base to the bill. Usually seen perched high in trees, it feeds mainly on fruit but also takes insects and other small animal prey. In Costa Rica, it is a widespread and commonly encountered resident.
value.classification: The Masked Tityra belongs to the family Tityridae, a group of Neotropical passerines related to cotingas and tyrant flycatchers. Several geographic subspecies are recognized, including Tityra semifasciata costaricensis in Costa Rica.
value.identification: Adults are mostly pale or silvery gray with darker wings, a blackish facial mask, and bare reddish or pinkish skin around the eye. The bill is thick, with a noticeably pinkish-red base and a darker tip. Males generally have a darker, more sharply contrasting head pattern, while females often show a browner head and mask. The bird has a broad-winged appearance and is often identified by its high perch, slow movements, and distinctive harsh, nasal, croaking calls.
value.rangeHabitat: The Masked Tityra ranges from Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is widespread and commonly recorded in both Caribbean and Pacific regions, including suitable areas of the Central Valley and foothills, generally from sea level to about 1,800 meters. It uses open or partly open habitats with mature trees, including forest edges, clearings, second growth, shade plantations, wooded savannas, and the canopy of lowland and lower montane forest.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally a year-round resident in Costa Rica and is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur in response to fruit availability or seasonal conditions.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from March through July. The species nests in tree cavities, often using old woodpecker holes or other natural openings, and lines the cavity with dead leaves, twigs, and plant fibers. Clutches usually contain two or three eggs. The female performs most or all incubation, while both adults help feed the young. Nests are commonly placed several meters above the ground in mature or partly open woodland.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms the main part of the diet, with berries and other tree fruits taken from the canopy and upper middle levels of vegetation. The Masked Tityra also eats insects and other invertebrates, and occasionally small lizards or similar prey. It usually forages alone, in pairs, or in small groups. Birds often sit quietly on exposed branches before picking food from nearby foliage or making short sallies to seize prey.
value.behavior: Masked Tityras spend much of their time perched quietly in the middle and upper levels of trees, where their pale bodies can be conspicuous against darker foliage. They may occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups and are not strongly associated with mixed-species feeding flocks. Their calls are commonly described as rough, nasal, wet, or croaking sounds. During courtship, males may move along branches with lowered or drooping wings while calling.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and common in much of its range, including Costa Rica.
